sentences.text: This bird possessed a disproportionately large head and jaws, featuring a skull that was flattened from top to bottom.
Ridges on the skull indicate it had a distinct frontal crest of feathers that was firmly attached and could not be raised or lowered.
Its head was evidently blue, while research suggests the beak may have been red with greyish or blackish plumage.
The broad-billed parrot likely went extinct around the 1680s, though the IUCN status system lists the extinction year as 1693.
Reports published in 1601 contain the first illustration of the bird alongside the first illustration of a dodo.
Dutch ships' journals from 1598 onwards first referred to the bird as the "Indian raven".
The species likely ate hard seeds from various Mauritian plants such as Latania loddigesii, Mimusops maxima, Sideroxylon grandiflorum, Diospyros egrettorium, and Pandanus utilis.
However, Holyoak argued based on radiographs that the bird had a weakly constructed mandible and likely fed on soft fruits instead of hard seeds.
Analysis of the underlying pencil sketch suggests the wings were not particularly short but appeared broad like forest-adapted species, with a large alula characteristic of slow-flying birds.
Historical accounts state the bird could fly with difficulty, and illustrations show it perched on trees, which is improbable for a flightless bird.
Although it may have fed on the ground and flown clumsily, its short and robust tarsometatarsus implies certain arboreal traits.
Hume stated in 2007 that the bird's poor flight, large size, and tameness made it easy prey for sailors and vulnerable to introduced crab-eating macaques and rats.
The broad-billed parrot is classified in the kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Aves, order Psittaciformes, family Psittacidae, subfamily Psittacinae, and tribe Psittaculini.
In 1987, British ornithologist Graham S. Cowles found the skulls were too distinct to be closely related to other species.
The broad-billed parrot was endemic to the island of Mauritius in the Mascarene Islands and lived during the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
Emile Oustalet argued in 1897 and France Staub as late as 1993 that the "Indian raven" was a hornbill, though no hornbill remains have been found on the island.
The taxonomic affinities of the broad-billed parrot remain undetermined.
Many authors, including the Newton brothers, inferred the bird was flightless based on the apparent short wings and large size in the 1601 sketch, though this is debated.
